content.title: About
content.content: Basbousa is a traditional Middle Eastern dessert consisting of a syrup‑soaked cake made from semolina, butter and sugar. The batter often includes nuts, coconut flakes or flavorings such as rose water or orange zest.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The name comes from the Arabic word “basbousa”, meaning “soft” or “fluffy”.
It is traditionally baked in square or diamond pans and topped with nuts or coconut.
Regional variations exist: Egyptian versions may use yogurt, while Turkish ones often add pistachios.
Basbousa is commonly served during holidays like Ramadan and Eid al‑Fitr.
The soaking syrup can be scented with rose water, orange blossom water (attar), or mint.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: Rich in carbohydrates and fats, basbousa provides a quick boost of energy, useful during fasting periods.

items.title: Calcium content
items.content: Butter and occasional dairy additions make the dessert a decent source of calcium for bone health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Semolina supplies B1 and B2 vitamins, which support metabolic processes.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Flavorings like rose water contain flavonoids that act as antioxidants.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Because it is sweet, people with diabetes or those watching their weight should consume basbousa in moderation.

items.title: Nut allergy
items.content: If nuts are included, they may trigger allergic reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Saturated fat
items.content: Butter adds saturated fat, which can affect cholesterol levels if eaten frequently.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Basbousa is served at room temperature, often alongside tea or coffee. Cut into bite‑size pieces, garnish with nuts, coconut, or fresh berries. Leftovers keep in the fridge and are best eaten within 2–3 days.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store basbousa in an airtight container in the refrigerator. For longer keeping, it can be frozen for up to 2 months after portioning.

bread-native-water-puerto-rican-style.title: Bread, native, water, Puerto Rican style

content.title: About
content.content: Puerto Rican native bread made with local wheat and water is a traditional loaf with a crisp crust and soft crumb. It is commonly used as a base for sandwiches, snacks, and classic dishes such as "mopongo".

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Traditional Puerto Rican bread is baked in open‑fire ovens, giving it a distinctive smoky aroma.
The classic recipe uses only three ingredients: flour, water and salt, without any leavening agents.
Bread is often served hot straight from the oven, sliced by hand.
In Puerto Rico the bread is a symbol of hospitality and is served at holidays and family gatherings.
A regional variation called "pan de coco" adds shredded coconut to the dough.

items.title: Source of complex carbohydrates
items.content: The bread provides sustained energy thanks to slowly digestible carbs.

items.title: Contains dietary fiber
items.content: Whole‑grain versions are rich in fiber, supporting digestive health.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: The traditional recipe contains no added fats, making it a low‑calorie option.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Wheat flour supplies thiamine, niacin and folate, important for metabolism.

items.title: Provides minerals
items.content: Bread supplies iron, magnesium and phosphorus, essential for blood and bone health.

items.title: Gluten intolerance
items.content: Wheat bread contains gluten, which can trigger reactions in people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: White bread can cause rapid blood‑sugar spikes, which is undesirable for diabetics.

items.title: Salt content
items.content: Traditional recipes may contain more salt than recommended for individuals with hypertension.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy the bread fresh, toast it, use it for sandwiches, or serve it with avocado, cheese or seafood. It is often brushed with butter or olive oil before serving.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the bread in a paper bag or cloth sack at room temperature for up to 2 days. For longer storage, wrap it in foil and refrigerate for up to 5 days or freeze in an airtight bag for up to 3 months.

content.title: About
content.content: Breaded chicken fillet is a tender chicken breast piece coated with a crispy breadcrumb crust seasoned with herbs and sometimes cheese. The product is ready for frying or baking and is commonly used in quick meals such as cutlets, nuggets, and burgers.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The breading helps keep the chicken fillet juicy by sealing in moisture.
In many countries the product is sold pre‑packaged in vacuum‑sealed bags for convenience.
Traditional breading includes breadcrumbs, salt, pepper, and often paprika or dried garlic.
Chicken fillet is one of the most popular protein sources worldwide, and the breading adds a textural contrast.
In some regions breaded fillet is served with tartar sauce or a honey‑mustard dip.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Chicken fillet provides high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Compared with many meat products, chicken fillet is low in fat, especially when cooked without added oil.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: It contains B3 (niacin) and B6, which support metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Contains minerals
items.content: Chicken fillet supplies phosphorus, selenium and zinc, important for bones and immunity.

items.title: Easily digestible
items.content: The protein in chicken fillet is quickly digested, making it suitable for light diets.

items.title: Chicken allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience allergic reactions to chicken proteins.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Ready‑made breading often contains salt; those monitoring sodium intake should check the label.

items.title: Trans fats in breading
items.content: If the coating is made with partially hydrogenated oils, it may contain trans fats, which are harmful to heart health.

items.title: Bacterial contamination
items.content: Raw chicken can be contaminated with Salmonella or Campylobacter; cook to an internal temperature of at least 75 °C.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The fillet can be pan‑fried, baked in the oven, or deep‑fried. Cook until the crust is golden and the interior reaches full doneness. Serve with vegetable sides, mashed potatoes, or in a sandwich.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in the refrigerator at 0–4 °C in its original packaging for 3‑5 days. For longer storage freeze at –18 °C, where it keeps quality for up to 2 months. Before cooking, check for off‑odors or discoloration.

content.title: About
content.content: Reduced‑sugar chocolate milk is made from whole cow’s milk and cocoa powder. The lower sugar content makes the drink less sweet while preserving a creamy texture and classic chocolate flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Sugar is typically reduced by 30‑40 % compared with regular chocolate milk.
The cocoa powder used is often enriched with antioxidants – flavonoids.
Whole milk provides higher levels of calcium and vitamin D than skimmed milk.
The beverage is marketed as a better option for children and active adults looking to cut sugar.
In some countries the product is certified as “low‑sugar” according to national regulations.

items.title: Rich in calcium
items.content: Whole milk is a good source of calcium, which supports bone and tooth health.

items.title: Contains vitamin D
items.content: Vitamin D enhances calcium absorption and supports immune function.

items.title: Cocoa flavonoids
items.content: Flavonoids have antioxidant properties and may contribute to cardiovascular health.

items.title: Reduced sugar content
items.content: Lower sugar helps control blood glucose levels and reduces the risk of dental caries.

items.title: Protein and fats
items.content: Whole milk provides a complete set of proteins and healthy fats needed for growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: People with lactose intolerance may experience discomfort after consuming the product.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Allergy to casein or whey requires complete avoidance of dairy products.

items.title: Fat content
items.content: Whole milk contains saturated fats; those monitoring fat intake should consider overall daily balance.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Although reduced, the product still contains carbohydrates, which is important for diabetics.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Chocolate milk can be enjoyed cold as a refreshing drink, added to smoothies, used in desserts, or poured over pancakes and waffles. For children, serve in modest portions.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in the refrigerator at 1‑4 °C. After opening, consume within 5‑7 days. Do not freeze, as the texture may change.

content.title: About
content.content: Plain muffin is a soft, mildly sweet quick‑bread made from wheat flour, eggs, milk, butter and a small amount of sugar. It has a tender crumb and a neutral flavor, making it an ideal base for a variety of toppings and fillings.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Muffins originated in England in the 19th century as a way to use up leftover batter.
Traditional plain muffins are often split and toasted to create a crisp exterior.
In the United States plain muffins are commonly used as the base for eggs Benedict.
The batter requires minimal mixing, which helps keep the crumb light and airy.
There are many variations—blueberry, chocolate chip, nut, etc.—but the plain version remains the most versatile.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: Muffins provide carbohydrates that quickly supply the body with energy.

items.title: Contains protein
items.content: Eggs and milk add a modest amount of animal protein.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Wheat flour and eggs supply B1, B2 and B6 vitamins, supporting metabolism.

items.title: Calcium
items.content: Milk contributes calcium, important for bones and teeth.

items.title: Low sodium
items.content: Plain muffins are typically made without added salt, making them suitable for moderate sodium intake.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Wheat flour contains gluten, which can trigger reactions in people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Although plain muffins are not overly sweet, they do contain sugar, which may be a concern for diabetics or those monitoring weight.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Butter and eggs make the muffin relatively calorie‑dense, so portion control is advisable.

items.title: Trans fats from improper fat choice
items.content: Using margarine instead of butter can introduce trans fats, which are undesirable for cardiovascular health.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Plain muffins can be enjoyed as a snack on their own, split and toasted with butter, jam, honey, or used as a base for sandwiches with ham, cheese, and vegetables.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store muffins in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 2 days. For longer keeping, refrigerate (up to 5 days) or freeze (up to 2 months). Reheat in the oven or toaster before serving to restore a crisp crust.
